newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy calls emergency, Albanian influx tops 10,000.
newsitem.headline: Italy calls emergency, Albanian influx tops 10,000.

text.p: Italy declared a national "state of emergency" on Wednesday to cope with a flood of refugees from Albania's turmoil as the influx swelled to more than 10,000 people in less than a week.

A special cabinet meeting also decided that genuine refugees would be allowed to stay in Italy for no more than three months and said Albanians "deemed to be a danger to public security" would be forcibly repatriated, a government statement said.
The first expulsions took place as the cabinet met.

Interior Minister Giorgio Napolitano told parliament that 289 "undesirables" were being flown from the southeastern port of Brindisi to Albania's capital Tirana in three giant Chinook army helicopters with crack paratroops guards on board.
He said the exodus from Albania had brought 10,619 people across the Adriatic to Italian ports in a ramshackle fleet of decrepit boats between March 13 and seven a.m. (0600 GMT) on Wednesday.

Albania, Europe's poorest country, has been rocked by unrest since the collapse in January of shady "get-rich-quick" savings schemes. The protests mushroomed this month into armed rebellion in the south and chaos has spread across the country.
Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini said a European Union plan to help Albania restore order and provide emergency relief was intended to favour a peaceful, political end to the chaos.
"It is also designed to ease the flow of refugees, whose consequences concern not only Italy but all of Europe," a government statement quoted Dini as telling the cabinet.

The centre-left government acted amid growing pressure from local authorities in the southeast and from the opposition to ensure that the refugees stayed no longer than necessary and that delinquents and illegal immigrants were sent back.

The "state of emergency", which will remain in force until June 30, will ease access to the emergency funds needed to care for the refugees and give wider decision-making powers to local authorities, political sources said.
Napolitano told parliament that Albanians would be carefully screened to ensure they were genuine refugees.
Those who were "the most exposed to dangers" in Albania would be allowed to stay in Italy for up to 60 days. Permits could be renewed for a further 3 days, he added.
It was unclear how refugees would be convinced to go home once conditions allowed.

Italy faced a severe crisis in 1991 when some 40,000 Albanians commandeered rusting freighters and poured across the Adriatic after the collapse of 45 years of Stalinist rule in the hope of jobs and wealth in Italy and elsewhere in Europe.
The country has since grappled with continuing problems of illegal Albanian immigration and drugs and arms-smuggling.
Several escaped prisoners from jails stormed in Albania's unrest and suspected mobsters have used the latest exodus to slip into Italy, according to ministers.
Italy also says racketeers in the Albanian port of Durres have hijacked the exodus, charging desperate emigrants up to $600 each for a place on a boat to a new life abroad.
The scale of the exodus has taken Italy by surprise.
"The wave and rhythm of arrivals from Albania...has exceeded every possible forecast," Napolitano said on Tuesday, adding that Italy had planned shelter for only 3,500 refugees.
Refugees continued to reach shore on Wednesday, including some 200 who had to be rescued by Italian coastguard vessels from a stricken Albanian tug 20 miles off the Albanian coast.
Coastguard sources said 60 to 70 percent of the Albanian naval and merchant fleet had already been used in the exodus. Those boats have been impounded on arrival in Italy.
